comparator.name: Bachelor Industrial Design Engineering
comparator.sourceNotes: The current official programme page and its linked 2026–2027 curriculum image were freshly retrieved and visually checked on 8 October 2026. The ordinary 180-EC pathway contains 115 EC of required study and 65 EC of profiling/choice. Year one is 60 EC required. Year two is semester three 30 EC required plus Design Project 4 at 10 EC and four distinct 5-EC profiling categories in semester four: Organisations, Skills, Technology and People. These 20 EC are categorized elective space, not compulsory fixed courses or interchangeable unrestricted choices. Year three is a genuine 30-EC minor, three final 5-EC elective slots and a 15-EC bachelor final design project. Five design projects total 55 EC; other required study totals 60 EC. All 25 stored components and their weights remain correct and unchanged. Named profiling slots preserve their category/slot restrictions without inventing optional content. The degree integrates people, organisations and technology through design projects; no formal specialization is inferred.

core: Human-centred product, service and systems design through iterative concept development
User needs, behaviour, perception and evidence-based design evaluation
Digital products, intelligent systems and computational prototyping
Organisations, strategy, customer value and innovation
Responsible and sustainable design, product lifetimes and circular systems
Design research, experimentation, communication and creative development
adjacent: Health and well-being as an application domain for human-centred design

trace: uses design thinking, customer validation and business-model development to move an idea toward a viable product or service
provides research design, experiments, surveys and statistics for investigating users and evaluating design claims
is the direct UCR product-development course: teams investigate needs, develop a concept and fabrication method, prototype, model and assess cost and sustainability
studies consumer psychology, customer trust, marketing strategy and responsible engagement around products and services
connects digital technologies to strategy, business-model change, foresight and responsible transformation
plans and executes customer research, analyses findings and communicates evidence for product and service decisions
examines cross-border governance, corporate responsibility and institutional constraints on sustainable innovation
develops organisational-behaviour knowledge about teams, culture, motivation and change needed for collaborative innovation
establishes brain-and-behaviour foundations for studying how people perceive, decide and act; it is not an ergonomics course
explains social cognition, attitudes, group processes and influence that shape user response and adoption
provides multivariate experimental analysis for evaluating human-behaviour and user-research evidence
studies sensory processing and goal-directed action as a cognitive foundation for human-centred interaction, without claiming product ergonomics training
applies framing, nudging, persuasion and ethics to real communication challenges around adoption and public response
develops experimental meaning-making across language, sound, performance and digital media as a creative communication contribution, not industrial-design visualisation
provides programming, testing and debugging foundations for digital product and service prototypes
provides calculus, vectors, matrices and modelling foundations used by robotics and computational systems
covers requirements, software design, testing, deployment and maintenance for reliable digital products
develops algorithm and data-structure design with performance analysis for computational product functionality
adds data cleaning, visualisation and project analysis for evidence-based product and service decisions
studies cameras, colour models, image processing and computer vision that can support visual digital systems; it is not interaction design
studies kinematics, motion planning, collision avoidance and robotic manipulation for intelligent physical systems
establishes planetary-boundary and sustainability concepts used to frame responsible products and services
adds chemistry and materials-science foundations and a greenwashing project for sustainability assessment
connects climate impacts, transport, construction, adaptation and mitigation to the systems in which products and services operate
directly evaluates products, processes and services across their life cycles and develops circular-economy strategies
develops evidence-checking for environmental claims so responsible design does not rest on misleading sustainability assertions
uses ecosystem-based design and planning to show how designed systems can work with natural processes
directly studies recycling, recovery and remediation as technical circularity and end-of-life strategies
examines collective decision-making, actors and policy that enable or constrain sustainability transitions
delivers a partner-facing technical and economic system-design project on cleaner energy
provides team-based applied sustainability research with external partners in a real regional system
analyses and produces climate communication for translating complex environmental problems to publics
provides ethical frameworks for responsibility, equality, future generations and environmental decisions

alternatives.label: Human-centred product innovation, digital systems & circular design
alternatives.labelReason: The curriculum contains one direct consumer-product-design project surrounded by substantial user/behaviour research, organisation and market study, software/data/robotics, creative communication, life-cycle analysis and ethics. The label names those supported strands and avoids implying a full industrial-design engineering studio curriculum.
alternatives.concept: A related-fields response that combines one substantial consumer-product-design project with user and market research, organisational innovation, software and data systems, robotics, creative communication, life-cycle assessment and ethics. It supports human-centred product and service innovation but does not reproduce TU Delft's repeated industrial-design studios, form-giving, CAD, manufacturing, ergonomics or integrated product-engineering sequence.
progression: Business, brain/behaviour, programming and mathematical foundations precede dependent marketing, software, robotics and advanced organisational work. Research Methods precedes Marketing and Consumer Engagement; Mathematical Methods precedes Robotics; Introduction to Programming precedes Software Development and Algorithms. Consumer Product Design appears after market, research, digital and sustainability foundations. Every course is offered in its assigned term, and the schedule contains 24 unique courses, four per semester, Year-1 PPD and six 300-level courses.

alternatives.label: Circular product-service systems & sustainable transitions
alternatives.labelReason: The curriculum retains product design, customer research and organisational strategy but replaces the closest route's digital-system cluster with a ten-course sustainability, circularity, governance and climate-communication cluster. The label reflects that material shift without claiming an industrial-design or environmental-engineering degree.
alternatives.concept: A sustainable-design direction that keeps product development, users, markets and organisations while concentrating on life-cycle assessment, circularity, climate, materials, renewable-system design, governance, applied sustainability research and public communication. It approaches product-service systems through environmental transition rather than through the closest route's digital-product technology.
alternatives.distinctness: The alternatives share 14 courses. This route replaces the closest route's ten-course brain/perception, creative-media and digital-system cluster (Introduction to Brain & Behavior, Perception & Action, Creative Communication Laboratory, Introduction to Programming, Mathematical Methods, Software Development, Algorithms & Data Structures, Introduction to Data Science, Image Processing & Computer Vision and Robotics) with ten courses in sustainability foundations, climate, circular recovery, governance, renewable-system design, applied sustainability research, climate communication and international business responsibility. Each direction therefore has 75 EC not present in the other.
progression: Sustainability Essentials I precedes Sustainability Essentials II; both precede Renewable System Design and R3. Business and research foundations precede marketing, strategy, market research, organisational psychology and international business. The life-cycle and climate foundations precede later system design, recovery, governance and partner research. Every course is offered in its assigned term, and the schedule contains 24 unique courses, four per semester, Year-1 PPD and eight 300-level courses.

candidates.label: Circular product-service systems and sustainable transitions
Health and well-being design
candidates.reason: The target supports health and well-being as one design application, but UCR has no health-design, service-design, ergonomics, usability or medical-product studio sequence. Adding biomedical and psychology courses would create a health-science programme around one consumer-product course, not a distinct 23-course non-PPD design curriculum.

selection.assessment: The first alternative is the strongest complete UCR response to the programme's integrated people, organisation and technology identity, presented honestly as related fields rather than as an industrial-design substitute. The second is independently generated by four direct sustainability/circular-design interests and changes ten courses toward environmental systems and transitions. A health-and-well-being design candidate was considered next, but the single application direction cannot support a distinct complete UCR design curriculum without substituting general biomedicine and psychology for absent health-design studios. Production stops at two alternatives.

blocks: Both investigate people and collect/analyse evidence for design decisions; UCR Market Research retains a customer and business framing rather than reproducing TU Delft's full design-research methodology.
Both address people and action in designed situations; UCR supplies cognitive-neuroscience foundations, not TU Delft's broader human-centred design and ergonomics formation.
UCR has no dedicated Understanding Design course or cumulative industrial-design theory sequence.
Programming and image processing do not reproduce a digital-interface and interaction-design course.

Both use an iterative team product-development project involving users, concepts, prototypes and feasibility; UCR has one such course and does not reproduce TU Delft's cumulative five-project studio spine.
Both develop future-oriented innovation reasoning; UCR approaches this through digital strategy and business-model transformation rather than industrial-design foresight practice.
Both address organisations, teams and organisational dynamics; UCR does so through organisational psychology rather than design-organisation integration.
Consumer Product Design contains limited fabrication and prototyping, but UCR has no separate product-engineering progression.
Both establish data handling and analysis foundations; UCR's course is broader and cross-disciplinary.
Robotics directly studies computational motion and manipulation for intelligent physical systems, but it does not reproduce the target's integrated intelligent-product design course.
Both assess sustainability impacts in product and system decisions; UCR directly contributes life-cycle and circular-economy analysis.
Both examine values and responsibility in decisions; UCR provides general ethical theory and applied ethics rather than design-specific value-sensitive design.
UCR has no dedicated product-engineering foundations course.
The compulsory 15-EC industrial-design final project has no scheduled UCR equivalent; optional UCR independent research is comparison-only.

notes.text: TU Delft Industrial Design Engineering is organised around five cumulative design projects plus dedicated design methods, visualisation, interaction, ergonomics, materials/manufacturing, product engineering and final-project formation. UCR can build coherent programmes around one consumer-product-design project with users, organisations, digital systems and sustainability, or around circular product-service transitions, but these are related-fields responses rather than a full industrial-design engineering curriculum.
